edges.description: Complete failure of pulmonary venous incorporation into the left atrium manifests anatomically as total anomalous pulmonary venous return.
Absence of direct pulmonary venous return to the left atrium makes right-to-left shunting of mixed right atrial blood obligatory to supply the left heart and systemic circulation.
Redirection of the entire pulmonary venous return to the right atrium and right ventricle recirculates oxygenated blood back to the lungs, producing severe right-sided chamber volume overload.
Abnormal anomalous drainage pathways can be narrowed or externally compressed along their course, raising pulmonary venous pressure and worsening postnatal compromise.

Mixing of desaturated systemic venous blood and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood in the right atrium with right-to-left shunting to the systemic circulation produces systemic arterial desaturation and cyanosis.
Restricted interatrial right-to-left shunting impairs left atrial and left ventricular preload, leading to low-output congestive heart failure.
Pulmonary overcirculation and right heart volume overload lead to neonatal congestive heart failure.
Chronic right ventricular volume and pressure overload progress to right ventricular failure.
Dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle from recirculated pulmonary venous return causes cardiomegaly.
Elevated right atrial and systemic venous pressures from right heart overload cause hepatic venous congestion and hepatomegaly.
Increased right-heart preload and heart failure physiology trigger compensatory tachycardia.
Pulmonary overcirculation and elevated right-sided filling pressures cause exertional dyspnea, including during feeding in infants.
Impaired cardiac output reserve and chronic heart failure physiology result in fatigue.
Obstructed pulmonary venous return worsens systemic desaturation and respiratory compromise.
Elevated pulmonary venous pressure and interstitial pulmonary edema cause acute neonatal respiratory distress and respiratory failure.
Back-pressure from obstructed pulmonary venous drainage and excessive pulmonary blood flow drive pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Severe pulmonary venous obstruction precipitates rapid neonatal cardiovascular decompensation and severe heart failure.
Hypoxemia and hemodynamic compromise from obstructed anomalous venous return trigger compensatory tachycardia.
Impaired pulmonary venous drainage and pulmonary vascular congestion produce exertional dyspnea, including during feeding in infants.
Reduced systemic oxygen delivery and cardiac output limitation result in fatigue.
Episodes of pulmonary venous congestion and pulmonary hypertensive crises manifest with paroxysmal dyspnea.
Severe pulmonary hypertension secondary to pulmonary venous obstruction increases right ventricular afterload and leads to right ventricular failure.
